newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS - Analysts say Thai data fail to lift gloom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Analysts say Thai data fail to lift gloom.

text.p: Thailand's central bank on Thursday announced lacklustre economic indicators which analysts said showed a sustained economic slowdown despite a moderate trade picture and smaller current account deficit.

They said Thailand's 4.8 percent year-on-year export growth in March, after 5.5 percent contraction in February, was offset by anemic private investment, a sharply widened balance of payments deficit and a decline in its foreign reserves.

Bank of Thailand governor Rerngchai Marakanond projected on Monday that exports, which rose only 1.5 percent in the first quarter, would increase 7.2 percent for the whole 1997 after a 0.2 percent decline in 1996.

Thailand has been hit by a sharp slowdown in exports growth and expectations of a decade-low economic growth rate of 5.9 percent in 1997 against 6.4 percent growth in 1996. The country's finance sector is troubled with over-exposure to the depressed, cash-strapped and glutted property sector and current high interest rates have stifled businesses.
Most analysts regarded the central bank's scaled down export target as optimistic, saying they expected foreign sale of Thai products to rise only four to five percent this year.

Central bank chief economist Kleothong Hetrakul said on Thursday the balance of payments deficit widened to 15.5 billion baht ($596 million) in April from 700 million in March. She declined to clarify the higher deficit.

Samarjit Shankar, BZW Asia chief economist, said the April deficit showed that Thailand remained under pressure from slackened inflows of short-term foreign capital. Kleothong said foreign reserves also fell to a 15-month low of $37.3 billion in April from $38.1 billion a month earlier.

Khanchit Assavasamrarn of Vickers Ballas and Co said he suspected that the wider April balance of payments deficit may stem from earlier central bank intervention to defend the baht in forward currency markets in February with the figure just showing up two months later.

Currency dealers speculated that the central bank might also have spent up to $10 billion in its market intervention to prop up the baht against heavy speculative attacks in mid-May. Some analysts were surprised by central bank adjustment of manufacturing and private investment statistics which showed a visible pick-up in industrial production in March although private investment remained sluggish.

The central bank said its manufacturing production index rose 6.4 percent year-on-year in March against a revised 3.0 percent growth in February. The bank earlier put the February figure at 2.4 percent.
It said private investment rose a steady 5.9 percent year-on-year in the same two months, its slowest pace since the second half of 1992.
"I am surprised by the adjustment of the two indexes which, if correct, suggest that the industrial sector slowdown may have bottomed out in February," said Vuth Puthamon of Multi-Credit Corp Plc.
Khanchit of Vickers Ballas said the more robust industrial output was in line with improved March exports of 126.9 billion baht, a monthly high since November 1995.

"But a one-month improvement should not be interpreted as the turning point for the export sector. We should see a clearer trend after the second quarter," he said. The central bank said although the March current account deficit of 15.9 billion baht widened slightly from February, it was the second lowest monthly figure in 35 months and sharply narrower than a 39.6 billion baht deficit a year ago.

The bank said first quarter trade deficit narrowed to about 83.0 billion baht from 114.5 billion a year ago but BZW Asia's Shankar attributed the smaller deficit largely to an import collapse rather than a meaningful export recovery. Thailand's business slowdown reduced first-quarter imports to 434.4 billion baht from 460.8 billion a year ago. ($1 = 26 baht)
